title: A 40-Year-Old Has $2.4M, No Mortgage And Spends About $45K A Year — ‘It Seems Like I Can Just Quit My Job’
detail:
A 40-Year-Old Has $2.4M, No Mortgage And Spends About $45K A Year — ‘It Seems Like I Can Just Quit My Job’
Image via Shutterstock
Casey B. Renner
Mon, September 21, 2026 at 8:15 AM CDT 8 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

One 40-year-old has been thinking seriously about leaving a job they hate and working part time instead. They have spent years saving for retirement, but now they're wondering whether they have already saved enough to make that change.

Retiring this early still scares them, especially when friends and family don't quite understand why they would stop working.

"It seems like I can just quit my job and wait until my retirement kicks in," they wrote on Reddit's r/personalfinance forum.

Don't Miss:

He Thought He Needed $88K To Invest In Real Estate. Then He Found A Way To Start With $100.

Real Estate Investing Without Buying A House? This 6-Month Strategy Is Offering 8% APY. Here's How The Private-Market Investment Works.

They Have $2.4 Million And No Mortgage. Is That Enough To Retire At 40?

The poster has $1.7 million in a brokerage account and another $700,000 in a Vanguard 401(k) they don't plan to touch until age 60. They have no kids, their house is paid off and after going through their expenses they estimated they spend about $45,000 a year.

For some commenters, that was enough to make retiring at 40 look realistic. One person looked at the $45,000 budget and said there was "no doubt" the 40-year-old original poster could retire.

Someone else pointed to the paid-off house and roughly $2.4 million in investments. "You have enough," they wrote.

Not everyone was convinced. Another commenter thought 40 was simply too early to walk away with that amount, especially when the money could need to last for decades. "I would not retire. I don't think it's enough," they wrote. "I know it sounds like a lot of money, but you have 40 years still ahead of you."

The $119,700 Income Estimate Could Make Quitting Look Easy. But What's The Catch?

The OP already has $200,000 in dividend and covered-call exchange-traded funds and plans to sell another $700,000 of individual stocks to bring that portfolio to $900,000.

Based on the current yields, they calculated that it could produce $119,700 a year before taxes. The OP spends about $45,000 a year, so on paper, the income would leave plenty of room.

"You may not be accounting for a market drop, in which case your dividend calculations will be totally thrown off," one person wrote. "Also, today's distribution doesn't guarantee future distributions."

title: They Have $17M At 43 And No Kids — But ‘It’s A Lot to Walk Away From’ With $5M On Stock Still Unvested
detail:
They Have $17M At 43 And No Kids — But ‘It’s A Lot to Walk Away From’ With $5M On Stock Still Unvested
savings calculation (Credit: Image via Shutterstock)
Casey B. Renner
Mon, September 21, 2026 at 9:00 AM CDT 7 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

A 43-year-old earns more than $400,000 a year and mostly enjoys their job. Still, quitting has been on their mind lately.

Walking away now, however, would mean leaving about $5 million in company stock on the table, with most of it set to vest over the next two years.

"It's a lot to walk away from," they shared on Reddit.

Don't Miss:

Warren Buffett once said, "If you don't find a way to make money while you sleep, you will work until you die." Here's how you can earn passive income with just $100.

There's More Than One Way To Put Cash To Work. Some Accredited Investors Are Looking Beyond Savings Accounts.

$17 Million Is A Lot Of Money. But How Much Of It Is Actually Available To Retire On?

The poster estimates their net worth at roughly $17 million. About $8 million is in retirement and investment accounts, another $2 million is in real estate that doesn't generate income, and $7 million is vested stock in the private startup where they work.

One person suggested planning around the $8 million until there was a way to turn the startup shares into cash.

"Unless there is a secondary market for you to sell your vested [pre-initial public offering] shares today and you actually trade for cash in hand, dubious to plan against that paper money," they wrote.

The original poster said there are liquidity events scheduled, so they expect to get some money out of those shares even if an IPO doesn't happen. "But certainly I don't count on all of it becoming liquid," the OP added.

The $5 Million Question: Is Two More Years Of Work Worth The Time?

The OP isn't trying to escape a job they hate. They mostly enjoy the work, which made sticking around a little longer seem reasonable to some people in the discussion.

"Two years is not forever maybe stick around if the job does not drain you and see if the IPO actually happens near the end of that," one person wrote.

Trending: Juan Valdez Just Went From 55 Target Stores To More Than 300. What's Behind The Colombian Coffee Brand's Rapid U.S. Expansion?

Others saw a bigger cost in waiting. "You are essentially taking a risk and buying time you will never get back with money you may never receive," another commenter said.

Unvested Startup Stock Can Look Like A Fortune Until It Doesn't

The OP's company could still be a few years away from an IPO. One person urged them not to count on the stock too soon.

"I have 7 figures of other stuff that vanished. Twice now actually," they wrote. "So just wait to count it when it's real."

title: My parents didn’t plan for retirement, but I’ve got millions: what’s the best way to help them?
detail:
My parents didn’t plan for retirement, but I’ve got millions: what’s the best way to help them?
Maurie Backman
Sun, September 20, 2026 at 3:16 PM CDT 8 min read
Quick Read

Paying parents' living costs through their mid-60s lets them delay Social Security to 70, locking in a permanent 24% monthly benefit boost.

Americans 60 and older lost $7.7 billion to financial scams in 2025, a 59% spike, making Trusted Contact Forms and Power of Attorney essential.

You can gift up to $19,000 per parent annually tax-free, or fund a diversified investment portfolio to generate income through their retirement years.

Two retirees, same $1 million, same 4% rule, buy one finished with $1.4 million, the other hit $0 in 12 years. Our free reader guide explains the flaw that separated them, and the income-first method built to avoid it.

Plenty of Americans retire comfortably after decades of disciplined saving. Others reach their 60s with almost nothing set aside, forced to lean heavily on Social Security checks to cover basic expenses. That gap between the two realities creates genuine financial hardship for millions of families, and it is more common than most people realize.

One poster on Reddit describes exactly this scenario. Their parents, now in their early 60s and still working, are beginning to slow down and think seriously about retirement. The problem: they have roughly $200,000 saved, which sounds substantial until you consider that it may need to stretch across 20 or more years of living expenses.

Canva | ajr_images from Getty Images and theboone from Getty Images Signature

Because the poster has significant wealth, they want to help their parents retire with dignity and some enjoyment. The question is how to structure that support wisely. Here are six strategies worth considering.

The 4% Rule is Broken, Built On A World That No Longer Exists

Every retiree knows about the 4% rule, but it frames retirement as a slow liquidation and still causes retirees with seven-figure accounts to agonize over a dinner out.

There's a different way to run the math that makes more sense today. Build an income floor — dividends, interest, and Social Security that cover your essential bills every month — and you never have to sell shares into a down market just to pay them.

Our free reader guide, The 4% Rule Is Broken, walks through it in about 15 minutes. Access the report here.

1. Gift Money Strategically or Build an Investment Portfolio

Direct cash gifts are the simplest option when you have funds to spare. In 2026, you can give up to $19,000 per recipient annually without triggering gift tax reporting requirements. Married couples can combine their exclusions to gift $38,000 per recipient. Amounts above that annual limit reduce your lifetime estate and gift tax exemption, which stands at $15 million per individual in 2026 following the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That exemption is now permanent and indexed for inflation starting in 2027, so the planning landscape is more stable than it has been in years.

title: Jim Cramer Says “Buy Reddit” (RDDT)
detail:
Jim Cramer Says “Buy Reddit” (RDDT)
Syeda Seirut Javed
Sat, September 19, 2026 at 2:33 PM CDT 3 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

During the September 17 episode of Mad Money, a caller asked why Reddit, Inc. (NYSE:RDDT) has remained range-bound and gradually drifted downward despite a long-term bullish outlook. Jim Cramer replied:

Alright, my take is that this is a $29 billion company. I think that there are companies that would pay $40 billion for just the book of business they have and be able to train all their different viewers and readers. Buy Reddit, period, end of story. Buy Reddit.

Jim Cramer on Credo (CRDO): “I Think You Can Buy the Stock”
Reddit Posts Strong Second-Quarter Growth

Reddit, Inc.'s (NYSE:RDDT) second-quarter results provide strong financial support for the growth argument. Revenue rose 61% year over year to $805 million, advertising revenue increased 64% to $762 million, and adjusted EBITDA more than doubled to $343 million. Daily active uniques increased 18% to 130.3 million, while weekly active uniques rose 24% to 514.6 million. The company also forecast third-quarter revenue of $860 million to $870 million and adjusted EBITDA of $385 million to $395 million.

At the September 8 Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference, CEO Steve Huffman said, "What is most valuable to Reddit is bringing users into the Reddit ecosystem. We want to grow our direct user base. That is where our business lives." He also discussed the company's efforts to grow its direct user base and convert mobile-web users into app users.

Bear Case: Traffic and Valuation

A risk worth mentioning is the composition of Reddit, Inc.'s (NYSE:RDDT) user growth. U.S. daily active uniques increased 6% year over year to 53.2 million in the second quarter, while logged-in U.S. daily active uniques rose only 1% to 23.1 million. International daily active uniques increased 28% to 77.1 million. Reddit reported second-quarter average revenue per unique of $11.85 in the U.S., compared with $2.26 internationally. Huffman said on September 8 that "traffic that is logged out or transient is just less meaningful to us," while Reddit is focused on growing its direct user base. He also said the company was continuing to work on converting mobile-web users into app users.

Valuation seems to leave less room for a slowdown. The company closed at $152.83 on September 17, giving it a market capitalization of approximately $29.4 billion. It also has a forward P/E of 23.31 as of September 17. The company is also investing heavily in its product. Huffman said the company considers its feed technology roughly 12 to 18 months behind the state of the art and that improving the feed is among its most important priorities over the next 12 to 18 months.
